claim.pdf_says: In the 5.2.4 operand table, the 'Expression' row lists three terms on three separate lines — 'arithmetic-expression-n' / 'boolean-expression-n' / 'conditional-expression-n' — and the 'User-defined word, including qualification and subscripting if needed' row lists three separate cross-references on three lines — '8.3.2.2, User-defined words' / '8.4.2.2, Qualification' / '8.4.2.3, Subscripts'.
claim.markdown_says:
| Expression | 8.8, Expressions | arithmetic-expression-n boolean-expression-n conditional-expression-n |
| User-defined word, including qualification and subscripting if needed | 8.3.2.2, User-defined words 8.4.2.2, Qualification 8.4.2.3, Subscripts | Any of the types listed in 8.3.2.2 suffixed by -n |
claim.why_it_matters: The line boundaries that separate the list items inside those two cells are gone, so three distinct terms and three distinct cross-references each read as one run-on string. 'User-defined words 8.4.2.2' in particular reads as though 8.4.2.2 were part of the preceding title. The item text itself is intact, so this is presentational, but it degrades an otherwise machine-readable normative table.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED. Rendered page 58 at 300 dpi and cropped both rows to inspect the printed glyphs directly. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING AND NOTHING IS MISPLACED. Every token the PDF prints in those two cells is present in the markdown, in the same order, in the same cell, in the same row, in the same column. The markdown table rows on lines 21 and 25 of page-58.md reproduce 'arithmetic-expression-n boolean-expression-n conditional-expression-n' and '8.3.2.2, User-defined words 8.4.2.2, Qualification 8.4.2.3, Subscripts' in full. Nothing has migrated to a wrong cell, wrong row, or wrong section, so the asserted kind 'misplaced-content' does not describe the observation even on the claim's own account. The claim itself concedes 'The item text itself is intact, so this is presentational.' (2) THE 'LOST' SEPARATOR DOES NOT EXIST AS A GLYPH. Examining the crops: the Term cell of the Expression row shows three bare terms on three lines with NO bullet, NO leading dash, NO trailing comma, NO semicolon, NO 'or' — the sole separating device is a bare line break. The same is true of the three cross-references in the Described-in cell of the User-defined-word row. There is no printed character in the PDF that the transcription failed to carry across. (3) THE PDF USES THE IDENTICAL DEVICE FOR PURE WORD-WRAP, INSIDE THE SAME ROW. In the User-defined-word row, column 1 breaks over three lines ('User-defined word, including' / 'qualification and subscripting' / 'if needed') and column 3 breaks over two ('Any of the types listed in' / '8.3.2.2 suffixed by -n'). Those are unambiguously narrow-column word-wrap of a single phrase, and they are rendered with exactly the same bare line break as the alleged list items beside them. The three-line Described-in cell is likewise too wide to fit the column on one line, as is the three-line Term cell, so the breaks are equally explicable as wrap. The PDF supplies no signal distinguishing 'semantic list break' from 'wrap break' here. Joining all of them on whitespace is the correct and consistent treatment of wrapped lines, and the transcription applies it uniformly — including to the 'Exception name' row ('14.6.13.1.6, Exception-names and exception conditions' wrapped over two lines), which the claim does not flag, exposing the claim's own inconsistency about its criterion. (4) NO MEANING CHANGES. The normative content — which sections describe each operand type, and which term names each operand type takes — is fully preserved. The concatenated cross-reference string remains unambiguously parseable both by a human and mechanically: every reference begins with a dotted-numeric section number followed by a comma, so 'User-defined words 8.4.2.2' cannot be misread as a section title containing 8.4.2.2; '8.4.2.2' is plainly the start of the next reference. Likewise each of the three expression terms is a self-delimiting hyphenated token ending in '-n'. This falls squarely under the reject criteria: the text is present, the difference is line wrapping / formatting only, and it does not change meaning. A markdown table cell cannot contain a literal newline, so intra-cell wrap flattening is an inherent property of the table representation rather than a transcription defect. At most this is an optional presentational improvement (inserting
between the list items), not a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy.
